title: Design a Web Crawler
tagline: A polite, distributed crawler that fetches billions of pages without melting the internet — or itself.
summary: BFS frontier, politeness, dedup, distributed workers, traps.

paragraphs: A web crawler systematically downloads web pages, starting from a set of seed URLs and following links. It's used for search-engine indexing, web archiving, data mining, and monitoring. Scope it before designing — crawlers have wildly different requirements.

blocks.title: Functional
items: Given seed URLs, download the pages and extract links to discover new URLs.
Repeat: a giant breadth-first traversal of the web graph.
Store the page content (for an indexer or archive).

blocks.title: Non-functional
items: Scalable — must crawl billions of pages.
Polite — never hammer a single site; respect robots.txt and rate limits.
Robust — survive malformed HTML, crawler traps, slow servers, duplicate content.
Extensible — easy to add new content types or processing modules.
Freshness — re-crawl pages so the index doesn't go stale.

blocks.text: The two ideas that signal maturity here are politeness (you can crash a small website if you crawl it carelessly) and the scale of dedup (you'll see the same URL and the same content millions of times). Lead with those.

items.detail: Target 1B pages/month → 1e9 / 2.5e6 sec ≈ ~400 pages/sec average; design for 2× peak (~800/sec).
Average page ~500 KB compressed-ish → 1B × 500 KB = 500 TB/month of raw content. Store in blob storage (S3/HDFS), not a DB.
Billions of URLs queued. URLs are ~100 bytes → tens of GB of URLs in flight; mostly on disk, hot portion in memory.

paragraphs: At its core the crawler is a loop over a queue (the *URL frontier*): pop a URL, download it, extract links, push new URLs back. Everything else exists to make that loop scalable, polite, and robust.

blocks.caption: A pipeline of stages connected by the URL frontier and dedup checks.

items.title: Pop URL
items.detail: Take the next URL from the frontier (respecting priority and politeness).

items.title: DNS resolve + download
items.detail: Resolve the host (cache DNS!) and fetch the HTML over HTTP with timeouts.

items.title: Content-seen check
items.detail: Compute a checksum/hash of the content. If we've stored identical content before (mirror/duplicate), skip storing it.

items.title: Parse & extract links
items.detail: Parse HTML, extract outbound URLs, normalize them (resolve relative paths, strip fragments).

items.title: URL-seen filter
items.detail: For each extracted URL, check a 'URL seen' set (Bloom filter / hash store). If new, add to the frontier.

items.title: Store
items.detail: Write the page content to blob storage for downstream indexing.

paragraphs: The frontier is the heart of the design. It's not a simple FIFO queue — it must enforce *politeness* (don't overload any one host) and *priority* (crawl important/fresh pages first). The classic Mercator design uses two layers of queues.

items.detail: Maintain a set of queues where each queue maps to a single host, and a worker thread is bound to one queue. A queue is only dequeued after a polite delay (e.g., 1 request/sec per host). This guarantees we never hit one site with parallel requests.
A prioritizer assigns each URL a priority (based on PageRank, update frequency, freshness need) and routes it into one of N priority queues. Higher-priority queues are selected more often.
Billions of URLs won't fit in memory — keep the bulk on disk and buffer the head/tail in memory for speed.

blocks.title: Politeness is per-host, not global
blocks.text: Mapping each host to a dedicated queue handled by one worker is the trick: it serializes requests to a host (polite) while letting thousands of workers crawl thousands of different hosts in parallel (fast). Always check robots.txt first and cache it per host.

items.detail: Before queuing, check if a URL was already seen. A Bloom filter gives a memory-efficient probabilistic check (tiny false-positive rate, never false negatives) over billions of URLs; back it with a hash store for certainty if needed.
Different URLs often serve identical content (mirrors, www vs non-www, tracking params). Hash the content (e.g., MD5 / SimHash for near-duplicates) and skip storing duplicates.
Infinitely deep URLs (calendars, dynamically generated link mazes) can trap a crawler. Defend with max URL length, max depth per domain, and per-domain page caps.
Set timeouts on slow servers, handle malformed HTML gracefully, retry transient failures with backoff, and checkpoint frontier state so a crash doesn't lose progress.

blocks.title: DNS is a hidden bottleneck
blocks.text: DNS resolution is synchronous and slow (tens of ms). At hundreds of pages/sec it becomes a bottleneck. Cache DNS results aggressively and run a dedicated, possibly async, DNS resolver.

items.detail: Shard URLs across crawler workers by hash of the hostname (consistent hashing). This naturally keeps all of one host's URLs on one worker — preserving politeness — and balances load across the cluster.
Downloader → parser → storage are connected via message queues so each stage scales independently and slow stages apply backpressure rather than dropping work.
Re-crawl pages on a schedule weighted by how often they change (a news homepage hourly, a static archive monthly). Track last-modified / ETag to skip unchanged pages cheaply.
Raw pages → blob storage (S3/HDFS); extracted links/metadata → a scalable store; the 'seen' set → a distributed Bloom filter or key-value store.

blocks.text: If asked to extend it: mention focused/incremental crawling (only re-crawl changed pages), distributed coordination so two workers never crawl the same URL, and separating the crawl from the index build (the crawler produces a stream of pages; an offline pipeline builds the inverted index).

cheatsheet: Crawler = loop over a URL frontier: pop → download → parse → extract links → dedup → enqueue → store.
Politeness: map each host to a dedicated queue served by one worker + a per-host delay; always honor robots.txt.
Priority: front queues weighted by importance/freshness route URLs before the politeness (back) queues.
URL dedup with a Bloom filter (memory-efficient, no false negatives); content dedup with a content hash / SimHash.
Defend against traps (max depth, URL length, per-domain caps) and cache DNS (hidden bottleneck).
Distribute by hash(hostname) so politeness is preserved per worker; store raw pages in blob storage.
Freshness via scheduled re-crawls weighted by change rate; use ETag/Last-Modified to skip unchanged pages.

questions.prompt: How do you ensure your crawler is 'polite' and never overwhelms a single website, while still crawling fast overall?
questions.hint: Think about per-host serialization vs cross-host parallelism.
answer: Politeness is a *per-host* constraint, not a global one. The standard approach: maintain a set of back queues where each queue holds URLs for exactly one host, and bind each worker thread to a single queue. The worker dequeues a URL, fetches it, then waits a politeness delay (e.g., 1 request/sec, or derive it from the site's response time) before taking the next. Because one host maps to one queue served by one worker, requests to that host are serialized — we never hit it in parallel.

Crucially, this doesn't slow the whole crawler: we run thousands of workers, each handling a different host, so we crawl thousands of sites concurrently while staying polite to each. We also fetch and cache robots.txt per host and obey its Crawl-delay and disallow rules. When sharding across machines, we shard by hash(hostname) so all of a host's URLs land on the same worker, preserving this guarantee.
keyPoints: Per-host queue served by one worker → serialized requests per host
Politeness delay between requests (respect robots.txt Crawl-delay)
Thousands of workers over thousands of hosts → still fast
Shard by hash(hostname) to keep the per-host guarantee across machines
followUps: How would you dynamically tune the politeness delay based on a server's response time or error rate?

questions.prompt: You need to check whether a URL has already been seen, across billions of URLs. Why use a Bloom filter, and what's the catch?
questions.hint: Probabilistic set membership with bounded memory.
answer: A hash set of billions of URLs would consume huge memory (hundreds of GB). A Bloom filter is a compact probabilistic structure that answers 'have I seen this?' using a bit array and k hash functions, at a fixed small cost per element (a few bits). It never produces false negatives — if it says 'not seen', the URL is genuinely new — which is exactly the guarantee we need so we don't drop new URLs.

The catch is false positives: it may occasionally say 'seen' for a URL we haven't actually crawled, causing us to skip it. We tune the bit-array size and number of hashes to keep the false-positive rate tiny (e.g., <1%), accepting that we'll miss a negligible fraction of pages. If we need certainty, we back the Bloom filter with an authoritative hash store: the Bloom filter is a fast front-line filter, and only on a 'maybe seen' do we consult the store.
keyPoints: Hash set of billions of URLs = too much memory
Bloom filter: bounded memory, no false negatives (won't drop new URLs)
Trade-off: small false-positive rate → skip a tiny fraction of pages
Back with an authoritative store if exactness is required
followUps: How does content-level dedup (same page, different URL) differ, and what hashing would you use for near-duplicates?
